title: The flow state
hookLine: Csikszentmihalyi's research on "flow": deep absorption when challenge meets skill

lines: A CLIMBER, A SURGEON, A PLAYER.
cards: A rock climber halfway up a wall. A surgeon in the middle of an operation. A chess player deep in a game.
A teenager on the last level of a video game. Ask any of them later what happened to the time, and they may shrug: it vanished.

A psychologist named Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi spent years asking people like this to describe their best moments at work and at play. Their answers kept sounding alike, and he gave the shared experience a name.

teach.b: He chose the word flow because people kept reaching for it: they said it felt like being carried by a current. First, the balance. Flow tends to show up when the challenge in front of you matches your skill.
Too easy, and you get bored. Too hard, and you get anxious. In the narrow channel between, attention locks on.
That's why Levin's first clumsy strokes felt like misery and the later ones like a gift: his skill caught up with the task. Second, the conditions.
In his telling, flow comes more easily when the goal is clear and you can see right away how you're doing. The climber knows if the hold is good. The cook tastes the sauce.
Vague tasks with slow feedback rarely absorb anyone. Third, what goes missing.

People in flow report that the voice watching and judging them goes quiet for a while, and time stretches or shrinks. They aren't thinking about themselves at all; the pride, if it comes, comes later.
Fourth, why it matters. Csikszentmihalyi found that people often reported these moments at work more than in their leisure, which surprised him.
So a meaningful day may not need less work, but work shaped so that it can absorb you.
Science can describe the state. It can't say what it means. Some people on spiritual paths see in flow a small taste of what contemplatives describe; others simply enjoy it.

how: People who look for flow often shape a task deliberately: a clear goal, quick feedback, and a challenge matched to their skill, then they protect a stretch of time from interruptions.

o: a meditation teacher who coined the word mindfulness
the psychologist who named flow, deep absorption in a task
a philosopher who said hard work is its own reward

games.q: what makes flow — tap the pairs.

s: in flow, people feel proud of themselves in the moment
the watching self goes quiet; any pride comes later.
Csikszentmihalyi found people often reported flow at work, not only at play
it surprised him, and it means work can be shaped to absorb us.
science shows that flow is a spiritual experience
science can describe the state; what it means is left to each person and path.

games.q: you're bored at a task you've done a hundred times. by Csikszentmihalyi's map, what moves you toward flow?
o: make it harder, or set a clear new goal.
do it while checking your phone.
games.why: boredom means the challenge has fallen below your skill. raising it, with a clear goal and quick feedback, moves you back into the channel.

practice: Breathe in for a count of four and out for a count of six: a clear goal, with feedback the moment you lose count, and when you do, start again at one, without comment.
If that feels too easy, try five and seven; if it feels strained, try three and five. Find the channel between bored and anxious, and stay there.

wordCard.voice: Csikszentmihalyi. The psychologist who named flow: deep absorption when a clear task meets the right level of skill. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: absorbed. Challenge meeting skill, until the time disappears on its own. See you tomorrow.
